question.problem:
Consider the polar curve $r=8{sin}^{3}⁡\theta -8{sin}^{5}⁡\theta $ for $\theta \in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ Given that 

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=16{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1),
$$

and ${y}^{′}(0)=0,$ which of the following statements are true?

I. ${x}^{′}(0)=0$

II. ${lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\infty $

III. The curve has a vertical tangent at $\theta =0$
question.worked_solution:
For a given polar curve, there is a vertical tangent at $\theta ={\theta }_{0}$ if

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}{{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})}
$$

is infinite. This means that

$$
{y}^{′}({\theta }_{0})\ne 0\,\text{and}\,{x}^{′}({\theta }_{0})=0.
$$

However, if the curve is continuous at ${\theta }_{0}$ yet the derivative takes the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}$ at this point, we say that the curve has a vertical tangent at this point if

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty \,\text{and}\,{lim}_{\theta \to {\theta }_{0}^{+}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\pm \infty .
$$

In this case, we're told that ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Substituting $\theta =0$ into the expression for ${x}^{′}(\theta ),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(0) & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot 0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Computing the limit as $\theta \to {0}^{-},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{16{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{16{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{16{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{16{sin}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{24{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{16{sin}^{\cancel{3}}⁡\theta \cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }(3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{24\cancel{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{cos}^{\cancel{2}}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to {0}^{-}}(\frac{16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (3{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1)}{24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}) \\  & =\frac{16\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)(3{cos}^{2}⁡(0)-1)}{24\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)} \\  & =\frac{0}{24} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since the right limit of our derivative is not infinite, the curve does *not* have a vertical tangent at $\theta =0.$ In fact, it is a horizontal tangent.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227801/assets/4a525b9a7a04f228bb45dc8c0c1cb916d1e98d8907e5fb1411ea52eb964c96ef.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
